Late Oct — Thai–Myanmar border: Thai villagers protested after stray artillery shells fired from the fighting in Myanmar landed on the Thai side (BNI, 28 Oct). No casualties were reported.

17 Oct — Sri Sakhon, Narathiwat: The most recent lethal Deep South incident found. A police officer and at least one suspected insurgent were killed and two rangers wounded in a gun battle during a raid on a hideout; no new fatal insurgent attack was found for 22–29 Oct.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Violence is confined to one area and no lethal incident was found this week, but the insurgency has not genuinely diminished. Over the next 90 days, the Thai–Cambodian land ceasefire is likely to hold, with the maritime dispute moving through conciliation and bilateral talks; legacy landmines keep a small risk of casualties. In the Deep South, expect intermittent ambushes, raids and bombings while Bangkok reshapes the peace process with a new Malaysian facilitator and possibly more interlocutors. Spillover from Myanmar's civil war on the western border is a minor additional risk. A sustained wave of coordinated mass-casualty attacks would warrant reassessment.

countries.name: Bangladesh
incidents: 27–28 Oct — Bibirbagichha, Jatrabari, Dhaka: Two pickup drivers, Jony (32) and Md Nishat (27), were beaten by a group on suspicion of mugging. Jony died at the scene and Nishat died at Dhaka Medical College Hospital on 28 Oct. The Daily Star counts at least 15 mob-beating deaths reported nationwide in October.

26 Oct — Khulna: Police data showed 71 killings in Khulna between January and 26 Oct, 23 of them shootings, which police link to rivalries among nine criminal gangs over arms and drug trafficking and extortion. An ex-Jubo Dal leader was among two people shot in separate incidents in the city.

21 Oct — Dhaka: Alam Sheikh, a migrant worker with reported mental-health issues, was beaten to death by a mob at Shaheed Suhrawardy Hospital on suspicion of kidnapping. Rights groups dispute the government's figure of 40 mob deaths in January–September; ASK counts 171 and HRSS 187.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Violence is deadly but criminal, mob and factional rather than organised armed conflict. Over the next 90 days, expect continued mob killings, gang shootings in Khulna and other cities, BNP factional clashes, sharper BNP–Jamaat polarisation over the Awami League question, and sporadic Awami League protests met by arrests. An upgrade would be warranted if the ICT death sentences are carried out, if moves on Awami League reconciliation trigger street violence, or if unrest becomes widely lethal.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
incidents: 28–29 Oct — Homagama / Kobeigane: The Human Rights Commission opened an inquiry and summoned officers over a custodial death in Homagama, and the station's HQI was suspended. A second suspect died after being handed over to Kobeigane police, and five villagers were arrested.

20 Oct — Moratuwa: Gunmen arriving by car shot a restaurant owner at his cash desk and fled. He died at Kalubowila Teaching Hospital and a woman was injured, and police released CCTV footage on 21 Oct.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Over the next 90 days, Sri Lanka's security situation will remain dominated by underworld and narcotics-linked contract shootings in the Western and Southern provinces. These will be met by police and STF raids under the anti-drug drive, with continued scrutiny of custodial deaths and police shootouts. No indicators of insurgent, terrorist or communal conflict were observed.

regions.name: Americas
overview: Haiti's gangs have turned the international force into a target, and the response is escalating. Four Salvadoran technicians of the Gang Suppression Force are still missing after the 18 October ambush in Croix-des-Bouquets. El Salvador flew in a rescue contingent of about 450 troops on 22–23 October, and a Haitian official spoke of up to 1,000. Burned remains handed to the GSF on 24–25 October have not been identified, and President Bukele says they are not his men. The UN describes gangs adapting their tactics, with more hostage-taking and reprisals against civilians, while elections remain postponed indefinitely.

Colombia's government has shifted to an air campaign. A bombing raid in El Tambo (Cauca) on 22 October killed ten ELN members, including two regional commanders, and on 28 October President De la Espriella ordered a sixth bombing, against Mordisco-linked dissidents, with results not yet disclosed. Armed groups keep up drone and ground attacks: a naval infantryman was killed in a drone strike on a Navy boat in Guapi on 23 October, and a soldier was killed near Santa Marta the same day.

Criminal violence along the Andean–Pacific belt shows no sign of easing. In Ecuador, 16 prisoners died in four prisons in a week, eight of them in two riots in Cotopaxi and Quito on 22 October, and at least ten contract killings were recorded in a single day on 28 October. In Peru, the state of emergency in Lima and Callao was extended for the fifth time this year from 28 October, while mototaxi drivers were shot dead in Rimac (24 October) and Puente Piedra (28 October) amid suspected extortion.

Political contests are intensifying without serious violence. In Venezuela, the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years on 22 October passed peacefully but ended with SEBIN detaining seven people, and Machado returned from exile on 25 October to crowds in Lara and Caracas. The government is mocking the return as a 'show' rather than arresting her, and Washington says stability must come before elections. In Bolivia, Morales-aligned groups paused their Cochabamba march under police pressure and now plan a national march on La Paz in early November. In the Dominican Republic, about 11,000 troops are deployed on the Haiti border, with two more battalions and artillery on the way.

countries.name: Venezuela
incidents: 25 Oct — Lara and Caracas: Maria Corina Machado returned after about ten months in exile, appearing at a church in Lara before a caravan to Caracas, where hundreds of supporters surrounded her car. She had been blocked at least seven times between June and September.

26 Oct — Caracas: Diosdado Cabello said 'there is no persecution' in Venezuela and told Machado to 'drop the show'. Acting President Delcy Rodriguez also called the return a show; no move to arrest her has been reported.

22 Oct — Caracas, Valencia, Maracay, San Cristobal, Maracaibo: Thousands joined the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years, demanding an election date, the release of political prisoners and Machado's return. The marches were peaceful, but SEBIN reportedly detained seven people afterwards, and opposition marchers in Caracas moved their rally away from a parallel PSUV march.

26–27 Oct — Washington/Caracas: Secretary of State Rubio credited US mediation for Machado's return and pressed Caracas on a timeline. US officials said they neither blocked nor helped her, and Washington's position is still that Venezuela must stabilise before elections.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. The week's flashpoints, mass opposition marches and Machado's return, passed without clashes or casualties, and repression stayed limited to targeted SEBIN detentions. This is political tension with limited violence. Machado's presence inside the country is now the main variable. The government has so far chosen ridicule over arrest, probably to protect the US rapprochement, but Cabello's earlier warning that she would have to 'answer' for backing the US operation against Maduro shows a hardline option remains. Over the next 90 days, expect larger rallies around Machado, pressure for an election date before July 2027, further short-term detentions of activists, and friction between Machado and the US-backed talks with the Rodriguez government. The border states remain exposed to ELN and FARC-dissident movement as Colombia steps up bombing raids. Upgrade to HIGH if Machado is arrested or attacked, if rallies are dispersed with casualties, or if colectivo violence becomes systematic.

countries.name: Colombia
incidents: 22 Oct — El Tambo, Cauca: Operation Onix, a pre-dawn bombing and ground raid on a camp of the ELN's Jose Maria Becerra Front, killed ten guerrillas, including regional commanders 'Marcos Pacifico' and 'Ochenta/Murillo', according to the president (the presidency's own statement said nine). It was the government's fifth bombing; earlier raids killed minors.

23 Oct — Guapi, Cauca: A drone dropped explosives on a Navy boat, killing a naval infantryman and wounding four. The attack was attributed to the dissident 'Jhonier Toro Arenas' 30th structure of the Bloque Occidental Jacobo Arenas. The same day, a soldier was killed by rifle and machine-gun fire during operations in Guachaca, near Santa Marta.

26–27 Oct — Suarez (Cauca) and Suaza (Huila): Armed men entered the Suarez hospital and killed a patient, and a clash in Suaza left six dead, five of them alleged extortionists reportedly killed by residents.

28 Oct — Undisclosed location and Bogota: The president ordered a sixth bombing, Operation Bosur-Kratos, against Mordisco-linked FARC dissidents, with no results released. A separate report said six Clan del Golfo members were killed in a bombing in Choco. The same night, police and troops launched an operation in Bogota's Santa Fe and San Bernardo neighbourhoods.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Fatal drone and ground attacks on security forces continue, and the government has moved to a sustained bombing campaign, with two raids this week and at least ten guerrillas killed. Armed groups still hold territory in Cauca, Catatumbo and Choco. This is sustained insurgency with regular deaths. The armed forces counted 176 drone attacks on security forces up to 1 October, more than in all of 2025, mostly by the ELN and Mordisco's dissidents. Over the next 90 days, expect further bombings, with the risk of killing forcibly recruited minors and drawing legal and political criticism, and retaliatory drone, sniper and explosive attacks on police stations, bases and riverine patrols in Cauca, Narino, Choco, Cesar and Norte de Santander. The pressure on the ELN may also push fighters toward the Venezuelan border. Watch for confirmed results of Bosur-Kratos, ELN retaliation after the loss of its Cauca commanders, and any mass-casualty drone attack in an urban area.

countries.name: Haiti
incidents: 22–27 Oct — Plaine du Cul-de-Sac: About 450 Salvadoran special forces arrived on 22–23 October to search for the four missing GSF technicians, and on 27 October a Haitian security official said about 1,000 had arrived; neither El Salvador nor the UN has confirmed that figure. President Bukele warned the gangs of consequences like those imposed on gangs in El Salvador.

24–25 Oct — Port-au-Prince airport: Burned remains recovered by the humanitarian group Hero Client Rescue were handed to the GSF at Toussaint Louverture airport. The New York Times said they may be the missing soldiers, but Bukele said 'they are not our men' and the GSF said the identities have not been confirmed.

21–25 Oct — Santo, Croix-des-Bouquets: The GSF and Haitian forces continued operations in the area held by the Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo gangs, which began on 21 October. No overall toll has been released. The GSF's special representative said hostile incidents against the force rose from two to fifteen in one month.

Late Oct — New York: UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu told the Security Council that gangs are adapting to the crackdown, with more hostage-taking and reprisals against civilians, and that 241 people were killed in the West and Artibonite for allegedly resisting gangs.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Gangs control most of Port-au-Prince and expanding rural areas, are attacking and possibly holding personnel of the international force, and are fighting off clearance operations in Croix-des-Bouquets. This is loss of state control over a significant part of the territory. The large Salvadoran deployment shifts the force toward a more aggressive, nationally driven operation. Over the next 90 days, expect intensified fighting in the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, with a high risk of civilian casualties and gang reprisals against communities suspected of cooperating. Identification of the remains, or a hostage or ransom scenario, will determine Bukele's response and could produce the deadliest GSF operation to date. Expect violence to keep spreading into rural communes and displacement to rise further. Watch for confirmation of the soldiers' fate, command-and-control friction between the Salvadoran contingent and the GSF, and spillover toward the Jimani border crossing.

countries.name: Cuba
incidents: 26 Oct — Nationwide: The Electric Union forecast an impact of up to 1,900 MW at evening peak, meaning extended blackouts across most of the island. Infobae counts eight total grid collapses so far in 2026.
26 Oct — Havana: Two members of the Opositores por una Nueva Republica movement were held for several hours and warned to stop organising meals for people in need, according to Infobae.

20–21 Oct — Santiago de Cuba: Residents of at least seven neighbourhoods took to the streets with pot-banging after more than 30 hours without power, according to Cubanet; no arrests were initially reported. The report has not been independently verified.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. There is no armed conflict, but the power grid still covers well under half of demand and the collapse of basic services keeps producing night-time protests, now again in Santiago de Cuba, while the state answers with detentions, fines and heavy sedition charges, including against minors in the Moron case. This fits the HIGH definition. Prisoners Defenders counts 1,351 political prisoners as of September. Over the next 90 days, another nationwide grid collapse is likely; each tends to trigger pot-banging, street blockades and targeted arrests. The security apparatus remains cohesive, and restoring power to protesting areas keeps unrest local. Sentencing in the Moron trial could become a new grievance. Upgrade to CRITICAL only if protests coordinate across several cities, security forces use lethal force, or state control visibly erodes. Watch also for migration pressure and changes in US fuel restrictions.

countries.name: Ecuador
incidents: 22 Oct — Cotopaxi and El Inca (Quito) prisons: Two riots left eight prisoners dead and ten injured. Over the week, 16 prisoners died in four prisons, including six strangled in their cells in Turi (Cuenca), which the Azuay governor linked to resistance to prison reclassification, and two in Loja.

28 Oct — Villa Club, Daule (Guayas): A contract killing took place in daylight on Avenida Leon Febres-Cordero. La Republica counted at least ten killings nationwide in a few hours, including at least four contract-style attacks in Guayaquil's Sur and Nueva Prosperina districts.

Oct 2026 — Nationwide: The Interior Ministry counts 6,890 intentional homicides since 1 January. That is below 2025, but the concentration of contract killings in Guayas, Manabi, Los Rios and El Oro keeps 2026 as the second-deadliest year on record.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Daily contract killings in the coastal provinces and a new wave of deadly prison riots confirm large-scale armed violence by gangs that the state treats as parties to an internal armed conflict. This meets the CRITICAL definition. The prison deaths show gangs resisting the reclassification programme, and further riots and in-cell killings are likely as transfers continue. The state of exception expires on 14 November and is likely to be extended or replaced by a renewed curfew. Over 90 days, expect continued US-supported operations against Los Lobos, Los Choneros and border groups such as Comandos de la Frontera, possible retaliation against security forces in Orellana and Sucumbios, and attacks on judges, prison staff, ex-police and local officials. Courthouses and prisons are the main risk points.

countries.name: Peru
incidents: 25–28 Oct — Lima/Callao: Supreme Decree 142-2026-PCM, published on 25 October, extended the state of emergency in Lima Metropolitana and Callao by 60 days from 28 October, citing homicide, contract killing and extortion. It is the fifth extension this year; police keep control of internal order with armed forces support.
24 Oct — Rimac, Lima: Mototaxi driver Giovanni Levano was shot dead at night. Police do not rule out a link to extortion payments.

28 Oct — Puente Piedra, Lima: Freddy Orlando Agreda Malqui, a driver for a transport company, was shot dead in front of a shop; the gunmen abandoned their car while fleeing. Police are considering a settling of scores or extortion.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Extortion networks keep killing transport workers in Lima every week, with two more fatal shootings of drivers in Rimac and Puente Piedra this week. This is recurring deadly violence by organised criminal groups, although the state has not lost territorial control. The fifth emergency extension, running to late December, keeps soldiers on the streets, but critics, including a former interior minister, say there is still no real anti-crime strategy and the killing rate has not changed. Over 90 days, expect continued weekly killings of drivers and mototaxi operators, more arrests of extortion cells, renewed strike threats from transport unions after high-profile killings, and pressure from President Fujimori's government to treat extortion gangs as terrorists. Upgrade triggers include attacks on candidates or officials, a mass-casualty extortion bombing, or violent clashes during a strike.

countries.name: Bolivia
incidents: 19 Oct — Cochabamba: Morales-aligned groups paused their planned mobilisation because of the police presence. Unions and social sectors still marched from Avenida Petrolera to the city centre against the diesel price rise and the decrees on state companies.

Late Oct — La Paz department: Morales-aligned sectors announced departmental protests and a national march from Patacamaya to La Paz in early November (reported for 6 or 9 November). The CSUTCB called mobilisations in all nine departmental capitals.

27 Oct — La Paz: The COB, which distances itself from the Morales camp's political marches, threatened its own mobilisations against the decentralisation of technical institutes and rising food prices.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Mobilisation against the economic measures continues, but this week brought no blockades, clashes or casualties, and police deterrence in Cochabamba appears to work for now. This remains political tension with limited violence. The risk is concentrated in early November, when the national march on La Paz could converge with possible COB action. The government has ruled out repealing the diesel decree and says it will not allow blockades, which raises the chance of forced clearances. The state of exception (to 17 December) gives the government the legal tools for that, but clearances on main highways or in the Chapare could produce casualties quickly, as in the deadly May–June blockades. Morales, under a terrorism arrest warrant, has an incentive to escalate. Return to HIGH if multi-day blockades resume, clearances cause deaths, or protests turn into calls for President Paz's resignation.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
incidents: 25 Oct — Haiti border: President Abinader announced that two more army battalions, with heavy equipment and artillery, are heading to the Haiti border to join about 11,000 troops already deployed. The Defence Ministry said the border stays open and border communities remain calm.

27–28 Oct — Nationwide: The Colectivo HaitianosRD said ten Haitians died at the hands of, or in the custody of, Dominican agents during migration operations between September 2025 and October 2026. The figures come from the group and have not been independently verified.

21 Sep–17 Oct — Border provinces: The army reported detaining 12,556 Haitians in irregular status along the border, 4,909 of them by the 4th Infantry Brigade, and migration authorities stepped up controls in late October.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. There was no organised armed or political violence inside the country this week. The military build-up on the border is a defensive response to fighting in Haiti's Croix-des-Bouquets, about 45 km from the Jimani crossing, and has not led to hostilities. Over the next 90 days, expect deportations to continue at more than a thousand a day, further troop reinforcements, and progress on the roughly 54 km of border fencing. The Salvadoran-led offensive near the border raises the risk of displacement and armed spillover toward Jimani, Dajabon and Elias Pina. The Dominican Republic will remain a cocaine transit point with joint US maritime interdictions. The main risks are humanitarian and rights criticism over deportations and deaths in custody, and diplomatic friction with Haiti, not internal instability. countries.name: Jamaica
incidents: 25 Oct — Fern Grove, St Ann: Brittania Reid (30), a US resident, was shot dead by a lone gunman at her father's nine-night (wake) near Ocho Rios. No motive has been established.
25 Oct — Blenheim, Hanover: Cleve Addiman was shot dead at home by a lone gunman, and his female companion was injured.
28 Oct — Portmore, St Catherine: Howard Hammond (44) was shot dead at a garage on Braeton main road; no motive has been established.

21 Oct — Kingston: Prime Minister Holness backed the police after the Sligoville gun battle, in which Constable Devoney Rose later died of his wounds, bringing the police toll to two. INDECOM counts 237 people fatally shot by police up to 16 October, matching the total for the first ten months of 2025.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Violence this week was individual criminal shootings rather than organised political or armed-group violence, and overall murders remain on course for a historic low. The Sligoville gun battle, now with two police officers dead, remains a serious but isolated confrontation, not a pattern of organised attacks on the state. The main tension is the high rate of police killings, already at last year's ten-month total by mid-October, and the rights debate around it. Over 90 days, expect further contested police shootings, possible retaliation against police in St Catherine, localized roadblock protests and continued scrutiny by INDECOM and Jamaicans for Justice. Watch for further planned ambushes on police, sustained unrest in Kingston/St Andrew or St Catherine, and late-season hurricane impacts.
